title: Playing under Stokowski and the Mardi Gras walk-off
summary: He finally played with Stokowski in New Orleans, where the conductor walked off during El Amor Brujo because of a Mardi Gras ball's noise next door; he admires Stokowski's phrasing.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: And what about, uh, Stokowski? Did you have a little bit of him? Oh, yeah.

Oh, it sounds good. I wonder if that's coming through the tape. I hope so. Yeah. Oh, you go ahead. Some more. After you. Okay. Yes, I did play with Leopold. And, uh, well, that was a long time ago. I'm noble. It took me a long time before I did get to play with Leopold, because, as a matter of fact, I never did play with him until he came to New Orleans here, and he made the famous walkout scene, you know? He came during Mardi Gras season, and you know how the auditorium is divided in two parts. Well, the small part was booked for the symphony concert, and the other part was booked for the Mardi Gras ball, you know? And we were doing Manuel de Falla something. El Amor Brudo, I think it was. And we kept hearing these noises of this band on the other side, you know? Chum, pa-chum, pa-chum, pa-chum. And, uh, well, uh, old Stokey didn't dig that, so he made a famous walk-off-the-stage scene, which made headlines. I enjoyed playing with him. I think he's a real slinging conductor. He...
